questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=3y-2x,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 3\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}(3y-2x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[3xy-{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $a=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}18 & =f(1,b)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 18 & =(3b-2\cdot 1)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ 4 & =3b-2 \\ 6 & =3b \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(1,2)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{D}y+{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2x}y+{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}y]_{y=x}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{x}^{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(8-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that is mind, let's now write the $y=-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2x-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}5r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [{r}^{5}]_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{5}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{5}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[-\frac{1}{6}{cos}^{6}⁡\theta ]}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}[{cos}^{6}⁡(0)-{cos}^{6}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}

Example: 
                    Finding Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y) =\dfrac{xy}2, \qquad
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2y, \: 0 \leq y \leq 4 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\frac{xy}{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[\frac{{x}^{2}y}{4}]_{x=0}^{x=2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=2.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}64 & =f(a,2)\cdot 16 \\ 64 & =\frac{a\cdot 2}{2}\cdot 16 \\ 64 & =16a \\ a & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\left( 4,2 \right) \in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a = 4.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157768/assets/a381fede820f9fc5ba08bb9569906d41a3e8f779de38b446c4f271ceef3a5ccd.png)

Notice that 

$$

$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({1}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[{sin}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =({sin}^{3}⁡(2\pi )-{sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})) \\  & =(0-(-1)) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{4}{\pi} \cdot 1 = \dfrac{4}{\pi}.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157768/assets/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

 

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

*If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157768/assets/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

 

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example.

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =28.\end{aligned}

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned}

tutorials.problem:
Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

*Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$
